record.paper_title: Some open problems in mathematical relativity
record.original_question: Can one define a sensible quasi-local mass that appears in nontrivial theorems, for example a theorem asserting that if a three-dimensional region of volume V has quasi-local mass at least a threshold M0 depending on V and other data, then every spacetime containing that region must contain a trapped surface and hence a black hole?

evidence.quote: Find a sensible notion of quasi-local mass which appears in non-trivial theorems such as; If a 3-dimensional region with volume V has QL-mass ;::: M 0 (V, ... ), then any spacetime containing this region must have a trapped surface and thus a black hole.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In general relativity, a quasi-local mass is a real-valued functional that assigns to a suitable bounded region (or its boundary 2-surface) inside a spacelike hypersurface of a spacetime a number intended to represent the total mass-energy contained in that region, depending only on geometric data of the region and its surroundings. A trapped surface in a 4-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime is a closed spacelike 2-surface such that both families of future-directed null geodesics emanating orthogonally from it are converging (i.e. both null mean curvatures are negative); by the Penrose singularity theorem, the presence of a trapped surface (together with the null energy condition and suitable causality assumptions) forces the existence of a singularity, interpreted as a black hole.

Problem. Construct a "sensible" notion of quasi-local mass m(Ω) for compact 3-dimensional regions Ω (with prescribed Riemannian metric and second fundamental form as initial data, satisfying the dominant energy condition) for which one can prove the following nontrivial theorem: there exists a threshold function M₀ = M₀(V, …), depending on the volume V = Vol(Ω) of Ω and possibly on a finite list of additional geometric quantities, such that whenever
   m(Ω) ≥ M₀(V, …),
every 4-dimensional spacetime (satisfying standard energy and causality conditions) into which Ω embeds as a portion of a Cauchy hypersurface must contain a trapped surface — and hence, by Penrose's theorem, a black hole.

Provide such a definition of quasi-local mass and a proof of the corresponding hoop-type theorem, or show that no such notion exists.
artifact.status_search_result: Defining a fully satisfactory quasi-local mass remains a long-standing open problem in mathematical relativity, originally highlighted by Penrose in 1982. Partial results exist: e.g. Yau (Comm. Math. Phys. 2007) and subsequent work derive lower bounds for Brown–York and Bartnik quasi-local mass implying the existence of horizons (apparent horizons / MOTS) for certain compact manifolds, giving Thorne hoop-conjecture-type statements. However, no universally accepted quasi-local mass with a clean general theorem of the threshold form requested (mass exceeding a volume-dependent bound forces a trapped surface in every spacetime extension) is known, and the problem is generally regarded as open.

status_evidence.title: Quasi-Local Mass and the Existence of Horizons
status_evidence.snippet: Lower bounds for the Brown–York and Bartnik quasi-local mass yield sufficient conditions for existence of horizons in certain compact manifolds with boundary.
status_evidence.claim: Partial results connect quasi-local mass lower bounds to existence of horizons, but a general threshold theorem of the desired form is not established.

status_evidence.title: Four lectures on quasi-local mass
status_evidence.snippet: Penrose identified defining quasi-local mass as one of the key problems in 1982; many proposals exist but none is universally accepted.
status_evidence.claim: The problem of finding a sensible quasi-local mass with strong theorems remains open.

status_evidence.title: Trapped surfaces (Senovilla)
status_evidence.snippet: Survey on trapped surfaces and their role in defining black holes quasi-locally.
status_evidence.claim: Trapped-surface criteria for black holes are active area; threshold-of-mass implications remain partial.
